Part 2 · Thinking like a physicist about the legacy of slavery

The hardest line to move

In 1870, five years after emancipation, freed people lived almost exactly where they had been enslaved. Watch what happens to that map over the next 154 years, measured two ways.

Press play and watch the left map. As the Great Migration carries millions of Black Southerners north and west, the whole region pales. Read only this map and you might conclude the pattern of 1860 is fading away.

Now watch the right map. It shows the same numbers, each divided by that year's regional average. It changes far more slowly. The counties that were darkest in 1870 are still the darkest in 1970, by nearly the same proportions. The migration drained most counties at a similar rate, so the region faded as a whole while the shape of the map largely held.

The readout below the maps measures that shape directly: the correlation between each year's relative map and 1870's. Between 1930 and 1970, as the region's average Black share fell by about a fifth, the match only dropped from 0.89 to 0.84. Today it is still 0.76. The amplitude collapsed; the shape eroded slowly and steadily, and it has never stopped resembling the map of 1870.

For the physicists: separation of variables

Write the Black share of county x in year t as a field n(x,t). Over 1870–1990 it factors almost exactly:

n(x,t) ≈ A(t) · f(x)

A single spatial mode f(x), shaped like the 1860 slavery map, carries about 89% of all county-by-decade variation; the time dependence lives in one regional amplitude A(t). A uniform loss term, ∂n/∂t = −k(t)·n, preserves any initial profile, because every profile is an eigenfunction of uniform decay. Only location-dependent terms, such as diffusion or advection toward cities, can reshape f(x). The left map shows A(t)f(x); the right map divides out A(t).

Part of a series on the contingency dynamics of slavery's legacy. Sources: IPUMS National Historical GIS; National Cancer Institute SEER county population estimates (Census Bureau, bridged race).
